claims.text: Similar-element substitution or addition that adjusts the effective atomic-size distribution will improve glass-forming ability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
The same intervention will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing alloys.
The targeted baseline phosphorus-containing alloys exhibit marginal glass formation and crystallize upon moderate thermal treatment.
The atomic-size-distribution parameter δ′ can be adjusted through similar-element substitution or addition and is related to lattice distortion and phase selection.

Replacing a primary transition metal with a chemically similar element of slightly different radius can reduce overall atomic-size mismatch without significantly changing the alloy's overall chemistry.
The intervention should be effective when rapid-quench processing is near the threshold of glass formation.
The benefit should be most pronounced when substitution reduces local lattice distortion without compromising chemical homogeneity.
Reducing atomic-size mismatch produces a narrower atomic-size distribution and reduced effective lattice distortion.
Reduced lattice distortion minimizes density fluctuations and heterogeneous nucleation sites that trigger crystallization.
Reducing atomic-size mismatch makes the local atomic environment more uniform.
A more uniform local environment lowers the driving force for local structural rearrangement and retards crystalline nucleation.
Retarded crystalline nucleation promotes a more stable amorphous structure and greater resistance to crystallization during heating.
The substituted alloy will have a larger critical casting thickness than an otherwise comparable unsubstituted phosphorus-containing alloy.
The substituted alloy will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than the unsubstituted baseline.
The intervention is unlikely to work when the baseline atomic-size mismatch is already minimal.
The intervention is unlikely to work if substitution introduces unwanted phases or otherwise significantly changes the alloy chemistry.
The intervention may not enhance stability when processing does not permit rapid quenching and amorphous solidification.
Interactions between phosphorus and the substituted elements could enhance or offset the predicted improvement.

contradictions.description: The conditions describe the baseline atomic-size dispersion as only marginally sufficient to stabilize the amorphous phase, while the intervention proposes narrowing that distribution further as the route to improved stability. The hypothesis does not reconcile why reducing an already marginal stabilizing dispersion would improve rather than undermine glass formation.
